title: Becoming an AI Engineer
subtitle: The Path from Software Engineer to AI Engineer

chapters.title: What an AI Engineer Is Responsible For
chapters.transfer: Architecture, ownership, interface design, and operational accountability remain the starting point.
topics: Distinguish using AI during software development from building software whose behavior depends on AI.
Map the overlapping responsibilities of software engineers, AI engineers, ML engineers, data engineers, researchers, and domain specialists.
Introduce the system lifecycle: problem definition, evidence, implementation, operation, and improvement.
Explain why a successful demonstration establishes only limited evidence of capability.
chapters.workshop: Annotate a support application's architecture and assign responsibility for data, decisions, measurements, user outcomes, and incidents.
chapters.failure: A persuasive demonstration answers one question correctly but fails on outdated documentation and has no accountable owner.
chapters.completion: Produce an ownership map that covers model behavior and the surrounding system, and explain what the demonstration did and did not establish.

chapters.title: Choosing a Problem Worth Solving
chapters.transfer: Requirements analysis becomes the basis for deciding which uncertainty the product can tolerate.
topics: Translate a user need into a bounded task with observable outcomes.
Compare conventional software, search, classical ML, and foundation-model approaches.
Identify error costs, acceptable latency, human review needs, data availability, and circumstances where automation should stop.
Separate business success from model metrics and convenient proxies.
chapters.workshop: Write the support system's problem brief and compare manual triage, rules, search, and model-powered assistance.
chapters.failure: A team maximizes automated ticket closure while customers repeatedly reopen incorrectly resolved tickets.
chapters.completion: Specify users, baseline, acceptance criteria, failure costs, and a reasoned proceed, restrict, or reject decision.

chapters.title: Build Your First Measurable AI Feature
chapters.transfer: API integration and defensive programming provide the structure for a minimal experiment.
topics: Implement ticket classification and structured extraction through a minimal model integration.
Introduce prompts, inputs, outputs, validation, timeouts, and basic usage accounting.
Compare results against a simple conventional baseline.
Collect representative examples and inspect failures before optimizing.
chapters.workshop: Build an offline rules baseline and a separate live-model path for classifying fictional requests and extracting product, issue, and urgency fields.
chapters.failure: A valid-looking response invents a customer identifier; another request times out and leaves no recorded result.
chapters.completion: Deliver a runnable feature, a small labeled development set, an error report, and measured latency and usage. Mark fixture replay separately from live inference.

chapters.title: Probability, Statistics, and Experimental Thinking
chapters.transfer: Testing discipline expands into statistical judgment about populations and repeated measurements.
topics: Teach distributions, conditional probability, expectation, variance, and sampling through application examples.
Explain precision, recall, thresholds, class imbalance, and asymmetric errors.
Introduce confidence intervals and comparisons between candidate systems.
Distinguish token likelihood, expressed confidence, and empirical reliability.
chapters.workshop: Compare two ticket classifiers using confusion matrices, paired cases, bootstrap intervals, and per-category results.
chapters.failure: An apparent improvement comes from a changed traffic mix; a second comes from repeatedly selecting the best result on the same test set.
chapters.completion: Explain both misleading comparisons, define the unit of sampling, report uncertainty, and defend a valid experiment.

chapters.title: Machine Learning Fundamentals for Software Engineers
chapters.transfer: Debugging and data modeling become tools for understanding what a model learns.
topics: Explain parameters, objectives, loss, optimization, training, and inference.
Introduce generalization, overfitting, regularization, and distribution shift.
Establish training, development, and test separation; demonstrate leakage.
Teach vectors, matrices, tensor shapes, and embeddings where the implementation needs them.
chapters.workshop: Train a small text classifier, inspect loss and held-out errors, and compare it with the rules baseline.
chapters.failure: Near-duplicate conversations or customer-specific labels appear in both training and evaluation data.
chapters.completion: Detect leakage, rebuild the split by the relevant grouping unit, and explain the difference between training success and generalization.

chapters.title: How Foundation Models Work—and Fail
chapters.transfer: Mechanistic debugging becomes more effective when the reader understands the model's computational ingredients.
topics: Build intuition for tokenization, embeddings, attention, transformers, and next-token prediction.
Distinguish pretraining, supervised adaptation, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning.
Explain context limits, decoding, reasoning-oriented inference, and computational tradeoffs.
Investigate unsupported claims, sensitivity to instructions, knowledge limitations, and inconsistent behavior.
chapters.workshop: Inspect tokenization and embedding behavior, trace a small attention example, and compare responses under controlled changes to input and decoding.
chapters.failure: A fluent explanation invents a product capability; a longer input causes a previously available fact to be missed.
chapters.completion: Connect observations to plausible mechanisms, preserve uncertainty, and avoid treating generated explanations as privileged access to internal computation.

chapters.title: Prompts, Structured Outputs, and Application Contracts
chapters.transfer: Contracts and validation remain essential even when an upstream component returns plausible prose.
topics: Design instructions, examples, task boundaries, and output specifications.
Separate syntactic validity from semantic correctness.
Handle refusals, missing fields, ambiguity, truncation, and unsupported requests.
Version prompts and compare changes against evidence.
chapters.workshop: Implement extraction with typed output, explicit unknown values, semantic checks, and a versioned prompt comparison.
chapters.failure: An output passes JSON validation but associates the request with the wrong tenant or invents a field value.
chapters.completion: Demonstrate that malformed and semantically invalid results cannot silently enter application state, and document unresolved ambiguities.

chapters.title: Designing Evaluation Data
chapters.transfer: Acceptance testing expands into sampling, annotation, and management of measurement data.
topics: Translate requirements and observed failures into evaluation cases.
Establish reference answers, rubrics, annotation instructions, and disagreement handling.
Cover representative traffic, difficult cases, important subgroups, and negative examples.
Protect held-out data and distinguish regression testing from capability exploration.
chapters.workshop: Build a documented evaluation collection, with separate development and holdout partitions and an adjudication log for ambiguous labels.
chapters.failure: A suite tests when retrieval should occur but contains no cases where retrieval is unnecessary or unauthorized.
chapters.completion: Explain sampling choices, label provenance, coverage, intended uses, and limitations so another engineer can maintain the collection.

chapters.title: Graders, Experiments, and Error Analysis
chapters.transfer: Debugging now includes checking whether the test instrument itself is wrong.
topics: Combine deterministic checks, human assessment, and model-based grading.
Calibrate judges against human references and inspect disagreement.
Use controlled comparisons, ablations, repeated trials, and error taxonomies.
Diagnose whether failures originate in the model, context, data, application, or evaluation.
chapters.workshop: Implement outcome checks and a rubric-based grader; compare grader decisions with human labels and reverse pairwise answer order.
chapters.failure: A judge prefers longer answers even when they contain unsupported claims; aggregate scores conceal a critical-category regression.
chapters.completion: Report judge agreement and error types, validate the comparison, and justify the next engineering change rather than merely report a score.

chapters.title: Selecting Models and System Approaches
chapters.transfer: Architecture decision records gain task-specific behavioral evidence.
topics: Construct a task-specific comparison across quality, latency, cost, operational constraints, and data handling.
Distinguish hosted access, available weights, licensing, and deployment responsibility.
Use public benchmarks as discovery signals and local evaluations as decision evidence.
Decide whether a failure calls for better instructions, retrieval, tools, adaptation, or a different task design.
chapters.workshop: Compare at least two candidates and the baseline using the same application cases and explicit constraints.
chapters.failure: A model with a stronger public benchmark performs worse on the support team's terminology or deployment requirements.
chapters.completion: Write a model-selection decision record, state evidence gaps, and define checks for future migrations. Recheck actual terms during implementation.

chapters.title: Data Engineering for AI Applications
chapters.transfer: ETL, database integrity, and access control become determinants of answer quality.
topics: Build ingestion, parsing, normalization, deduplication, and versioning pipelines.
Preserve document structure, source identifiers, provenance, and update history.
Carry access permissions into downstream retrieval and storage.
Handle deletions, stale content, conflicting sources, and corrupted documents.
chapters.workshop: Ingest a versioned fictional documentation corpus and retain tenant scope, effective dates, source anchors, and deletion records.
chapters.failure: A deleted article remains in the index, or parsing separates a warning from the procedure it qualifies.
chapters.completion: Produce an inspectable corpus and demonstrate correct propagation of updates, deletions, and permission changes.

chapters.title: Retrieval and Search Fundamentals
chapters.transfer: Search indexing and performance measurement extend to semantic representations.
topics: Explain lexical search, dense embeddings, similarity, approximate search, and hybrid retrieval.
Explore chunking, metadata filters, query rewriting, and reranking.
Measure retrieval separately from generated answers.
Diagnose vocabulary mismatch, weak coverage, distractors, and inappropriate filtering.
chapters.workshop: Compare lexical, dense, and hybrid retrieval on labeled questions, using recall at a fixed cutoff and ranked relevance measures.
chapters.failure: Exact error codes disappear under semantic matching, while paraphrased questions defeat a lexical-only baseline.
chapters.completion: Identify the errors each strategy fixes or introduces and preserve permission filtering throughout the comparison.

chapters.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Context Construction
chapters.transfer: Dependency management now includes the evidence supplied to the model.
topics: Assemble questions, instructions, retrieved evidence, and output requirements into useful context.
Connect generated claims to supporting passages.
Handle insufficient evidence, contradictory sources, and unanswerable questions.
Compare retrieval, long-context input, and hybrid approaches under a common evaluation.
chapters.workshop: Add document-grounded answers with source anchors; separately score retrieval, claim support, completeness, and abstention.
chapters.failure: A real citation does not support its adjacent claim, or two valid documents describe different product versions.
chapters.completion: Produce supported answers, abstain appropriately, and defend the context strategy under measured quality and resource constraints.

chapters.title: Conversation State, Memory, and Context Lifecycles
chapters.transfer: State modeling and retention rules remain distinct from the model's text history.
topics: Distinguish conversation history, application state, saved preferences, retrieved knowledge, and learned parameters.
Design memory creation, retrieval, correction, expiration, and deletion.
Compare summarization, selection, and reconstruction of context.
Test whether important information survives long interactions and whether obsolete information persists.
chapters.workshop: Implement inspectable session memory, user corrections, expiration, and reconstruction from authoritative application records.
chapters.failure: A compressed history loses a user constraint, or an outdated preference survives an explicit correction.
chapters.completion: Show correction and deletion working across subsequent calls; document what compaction preserves, loses, and cannot establish.

chapters.title: Designing Tools for Model Callers
chapters.transfer: API contracts, authorization, and least privilege constrain a new kind of caller.
topics: Define clear tool purposes, arguments, results, and error behavior.
Distinguish read operations, reversible changes, and consequential actions.
Enforce authorization, validation, and scoped credentials in application code.
Introduce tool interoperability and explain what a protocol does—and does not—guarantee.
chapters.workshop: Expose ticket lookup and draft creation with explicit tenant identity, permission checks, validation, and auditable results.
chapters.failure: The model supplies another tenant's identifier or treats a tool's descriptive text as permission to perform an action.
chapters.completion: Demonstrate rejection of unauthorized requests and invalid arguments independently of prompt compliance.

chapters.title: Reliable Model-Powered Workflows
chapters.transfer: State machines and distributed-systems recovery provide explicit control over uncertain steps.
topics: Combine models with explicit routing, state machines, parallel steps, and validation.
Handle retries, idempotency, timeouts, partial completion, and compensation.
Place human review at defined decision points.
Select model-driven decisions only where they provide measurable value.
chapters.workshop: Build a triage-to-draft workflow with review and restartable steps, using a simulated ticket service for mutations.
chapters.failure: A service commits an action but the response times out; blindly retrying would duplicate the action.
chapters.completion: Demonstrate interruption recovery, stable operation identifiers, and verified outcomes without duplicated side effects.

chapters.title: Agent Loops and Harness Engineering
chapters.transfer: Runtime design expands to governing model-selected actions and resource consumption.
topics: Explain the interaction among model, tools, observations, state, and stopping conditions.
Define the harness's responsibility for execution, permissions, resources, and recovery.
Introduce planning, replanning, bounded exploration, and escalation.
Compare a bounded agent with the existing explicit workflow.
chapters.workshop: Build an investigation agent that can inspect approved documentation and ticket state, create a draft, and escalate unresolved work.
chapters.failure: The agent loops after receiving no useful new evidence or attempts to act after exhausting its budget.
chapters.completion: Enforce action, time, and spending limits in code and measure whether flexibility improves completion under comparable constraints.

chapters.title: Long-Running Work and Multiple Agents
chapters.transfer: Checkpointing, concurrency, and ownership become essential for continuity and coordination.
topics: Persist goals, progress, artifacts, and checkpoints across sessions.
Reconstruct context and reconcile recorded progress with actual environment state.
Evaluate delegation, parallel research, specialization, and shared-state coordination.
Diagnose duplicated work, conflicting results, communication overhead, and cascading failures.
chapters.workshop: Resume a stopped investigation and compare a single investigator with bounded delegated research under the same total resource budget.
chapters.failure: Two workers duplicate a task or a resumed agent trusts a progress note that conflicts with the actual ticket state.
chapters.completion: Recover coherently, resolve conflicting work, and report both task outcomes and coordination overhead without assuming delegation is superior.

chapters.title: Evaluating Agents and Verifying Actions
chapters.transfer: End-to-end tests expand to repeated trials and inspection of external outcomes.
topics: Measure completion, prohibited actions, resource use, and consistency across trials.
Distinguish useful trajectory inspection from unnecessarily prescribing every step.
Verify actual database or environment changes independently of the agent's narration.
Build isolated test environments and examine simulator and grader limitations.
chapters.workshop: Run isolated agent trials with outcome checks, authorization checks, and a calibrated communication rubric.
chapters.failure: An agent reports success without changing state; another achieves the requested state through an unauthorized action.
chapters.completion: Detect both failures and distinguish first-attempt success, success with retries, and consistency across trials.

chapters.title: Fine-Tuning, Distillation, and Model Adaptation
chapters.transfer: Controlled releases and data discipline govern changes to model parameters.
topics: Determine whether an observed problem justifies changing model parameters.
Prepare adaptation data and protect independent evaluation.
Explain supervised fine-tuning, parameter-efficient adaptation, distillation, and preference-based methods.
Measure improvements alongside regressions, maintenance burden, and operational cost.
chapters.workshop: Adapt a small model for one support task or analyze supplied reproducible experiment records, comparing it with prompting and the original model.
chapters.failure: Task-specific accuracy improves while unsupported answers increase or training examples leak into evaluation.
chapters.completion: Defend adoption or rejection using independent results and maintenance costs; distinguish executed training from analysis of recorded results.

chapters.title: Inference and Hosting Fundamentals
chapters.transfer: Capacity planning and profiling apply to model memory and token generation.
topics: Explain memory requirements, numerical precision, quantization, and hardware constraints.
Introduce prefill, decoding, caching, batching, throughput, and tail latency.
Compare managed inference with operating available model weights.
Profile the actual workload before selecting optimizations.
chapters.workshop: Benchmark a small model or a supplied deployment environment across input lengths and concurrency levels, retaining quality checks.
chapters.failure: A configuration improves throughput while making interactive tail latency unacceptable, or reduces memory at the expense of task quality.
chapters.completion: Identify the limiting resource and justify a deployment configuration with measured tradeoffs and clear hardware assumptions.

chapters.title: Multimodal Systems: Documents, Images, Audio, and Video
chapters.transfer: Media pipelines introduce new input quality, alignment, and evaluation responsibilities.
topics: Extend the application to screenshots, scanned documents, and recorded support messages.
Compare direct multimodal processing with OCR, transcription, and specialist components.
Handle temporal alignment, missing modalities, image quality, and streaming interactions.
Introduce generated media, provenance, consent, and modality-specific evaluation.
chapters.workshop: Build a document-understanding extension; use a separate audio exercise to examine transcription and timing errors. Keep advanced video work in companion material.
chapters.failure: A text shortcut makes an image benchmark look successful even though the model ignores the image; a scan obscures a critical qualifier.
chapters.completion: Evaluate cases that require visual evidence, identify modality-specific errors, and trace output claims to the correct page, region, or time interval.

chapters.title: Security and Trust Boundaries
chapters.transfer: Threat modeling and defense in depth extend across model-visible content and tool execution.
topics: Threat-model prompts, retrieved documents, tool responses, dependencies, and generated outputs.
Address injection, information disclosure, unsafe output handling, excessive authority, and resource exhaustion.
Apply isolation, least privilege, secret protection, egress controls, and output validation.
Test defenses against realistic application-level attacks.
chapters.workshop: Attack and harden the fictional support service with malicious documents, cross-tenant requests, and unsafe output handling cases.
chapters.failure: A retrieved article instructs the agent to disclose private ticket content through an external tool.
chapters.completion: Show which attacks are prevented by enforced boundaries, record residual risks, and avoid claiming that finite testing proves immunity.

chapters.title: Human Interaction and Responsible Product Design
chapters.transfer: User experience and accountability become part of the system's error-handling design.
topics: Communicate capabilities and limitations in ways that help users act.
Support correction, dismissal, escalation, cancellation, and recovery.
Evaluate automation bias, inappropriate reliance, subgroup performance, and accessibility.
Define accountable ownership and collaborate with privacy, legal, security, and domain specialists.
chapters.workshop: Conduct a structured user walkthrough with a wrong answer, an ambiguous draft, and an interrupted task requiring human recovery.
chapters.failure: A nominal review step provides neither the evidence nor the controls a reviewer needs to catch an error.
chapters.completion: Demonstrate usable correction and recovery, identify affected users, and document unresolved risks and responsible owners.

chapters.title: Production Architecture and Release Engineering
chapters.transfer: Release engineering must account for behavioral dependencies beyond application code.
topics: Separate interactive requests, background jobs, ingestion, model access, and evaluation.
Version code, prompts, models, retrieval indexes, and relevant configuration together.
Design resource limits, graceful degradation, tenancy boundaries, and failure containment.
Release through staged exposure with behavioral checks and rollback procedures.
chapters.workshop: Package the support service with a release manifest and stage a candidate against a stable baseline in an isolated environment.
chapters.failure: A prompt update works with a new index but is accidentally deployed with the old one, or rollback would invalidate active work.
chapters.completion: Reproduce a release and rehearse a failed rollout while preserving user work and compatible state.

chapters.title: Observability, Debugging, and Incident Response
chapters.transfer: Tracing and incident analysis now include behavioral quality and sensitive context.
topics: Trace requests across model calls, retrieval, tools, and state changes.
Monitor outcome quality alongside availability and performance.
Collect useful diagnostics while controlling sensitive-data exposure and retention.
Reproduce failures, identify causes, respond to incidents, and turn findings into regression cases.
chapters.workshop: Investigate a planted routing or retrieval regression using versioned traces, user reports, and production-like evaluation.
chapters.failure: Availability remains healthy while a subset of users receives worse answers; indiscriminate logging would expose private data.
chapters.completion: Write a postmortem supported by evidence, demonstrate recovery, and add a targeted regression case without retaining unnecessary sensitive content.

chapters.title: Economics and Continuous Optimization
chapters.transfer: Performance engineering expands to total cost of successful service.
topics: Measure total cost per successfully completed task, including retries and human review.
Compare caching, routing, smaller models, batching, and reduced context.
Optimize quality, latency, and cost together; account for maintenance and resource consumption.
Reevaluate earlier optimizations when models, traffic, or requirements change.
chapters.workshop: Compare measured operating points for the support service and select an optimization subject to an explicit quality constraint.
chapters.failure: Lower token cost increases review work, or cached answers survive a documentation or permission change.
chapters.completion: Demonstrate a defensible improvement on held-out cases, count failed work, and state assumptions and uncertainty in cost estimates.

chapters.title: Capstone: From Working Application to Defensible System
chapters.transfer: Engineering review joins implementation, experimental evidence, and operational responsibility.
topics: Consolidate the application's requirements, architecture, data, evaluations, and operational controls.
Run a fresh acceptance set that includes ordinary work and difficult scenarios.
Conduct security, interruption, recovery, and model-change exercises.
Present remaining limitations and make a supported release decision.
chapters.workshop: Assemble the complete capstone evidence package and conduct an independent design and release review.
chapters.failure: The application passes a curated demo but fails fresh cases, exceeds its operating budget, or lacks a recovery path.
chapters.completion: Meet the published educational acceptance rubric or defend a restricted deployment or no-release decision with a remediation plan.

chapters.title: Working Effectively on an AI Engineering Team
chapters.transfer: Collaboration and review incorporate data, graders, and model behavior as maintained assets.
topics: Assign responsibility for product outcomes, datasets, evaluations, infrastructure, and incidents.
Review changes to prompts, data, graders, tools, and models.
Collaborate with domain experts to resolve ambiguous requirements and labels.
Maintain decision records and prioritize work from observed failures.
chapters.workshop: Review a proposed model upgrade with a domain reviewer, application owner, and operations owner; make the evidence and disagreement explicit.
chapters.failure: A team improves an evaluation score by changing the grader at the same time as the model, leaving the result uninterpretable.
chapters.completion: Lead a review that separates changes, resolves or records disagreements, and assigns accountable next actions.

chapters.title: Building Your Career and Continuing to Learn
chapters.transfer: Professional judgment is demonstrated through explainable decisions and reproducible work.
topics: Assess competence through systems built, failures diagnosed, and decisions defended.
Present a portfolio with reproducible experiments and operational evidence.
Read papers critically: task, baseline, method, result, limitations, and applicability.
Choose deeper paths in retrieval, evaluation, agent systems, model adaptation, inference infrastructure, multimodal systems, or security.
chapters.workshop: Write a portfolio case study and evaluate one new research result for relevance to the support application's observed failure modes.
chapters.failure: A portfolio presents a polished interface and benchmark headline but cannot explain the data, experiments, or deployment limitations.
chapters.completion: Demonstrate independent understanding and produce a learning plan linked to observed skill gaps, without claiming a guaranteed job outcome.
